decisions.reason: “Marched in formation beneath fluttering imperial banners” keeps the sense and voice.
The procession-centered phrasing preserves the carriage’s position and purpose.
The guards unleash a collective wave of qi; the singular preserves that sense.
“Slip from someone’s lips” keeps the source’s image.
“Who had said that?” naturally preserves the question about the unidentified voice.
The procession’s halt remains clear from context; the tightened phrasing keeps the action.
SOL drops the source’s emphasis that his presence is truly overwhelming.
SOL omits the source’s emphasis that Baek Yeon is unquestionably the Emperor’s right hand.
“Moved as one” naturally preserves the image of acting like a single body.
The dialogue’s progression makes the joining clear without “soon.”
The timing beat is retained in H012’s “It was then.”
“As the cheer faded” loses the source’s specific timing at the very end of the resounding cry.
Taking his place on the throne naturally conveys the empty seat being filled.
“For years” weakens the source’s emphasis on many long years of seclusion.
SOL adds that he rose through turbulent times, a claim not stated in the source.
The ellipsis preserves the stunned pause in natural English punctuation.
The ellipsis preserves the stunned pause in natural English punctuation.
“Shock and disquiet” swept over the hall like an invisible wave, keeping the source’s image.
SOL drops the officials’ “great and small” distinction and changes gleaming eyes to sharper eyes.
“Its very heart” naturally preserves the image of the officials as the empire’s center.
The bent backs and unbowed eyes retain the contrast in natural English.
“Across the hall” conveys the meeting of their gazes without an awkward literal image.
SOL changes the narrator’s uncertainty about people’s impression into a claim about what they heard.
SOL drops the source’s gradual thawing, “little by little.”
The melody and fluttering sleeves keep the source’s effect in natural prose.
“Perhaps” preserves the source’s hedge, and the nerves settling keeps its cause.
“Say the wrong thing” is an idiomatic recast that keeps the warning’s meaning.
The source identifies the food as anju, a dish accompanying drinks; SOL’s generic plate drops that detail.
“Fix me with an unusually persistent stare” preserves the sustained, attaching quality of his gaze.
“Too” naturally links the young official’s voice to the preceding observation.
The hall’s capacity and the officials’ distance remain intact in the tighter phrasing.
The concessive phrasing preserves that all the guards are masters while only a few stay near the Emperor.
“Holding their assigned positions” keeps the sense without the stiff “to.”
SOL omits that the man kept watching despite hearing the young official’s explanation.
The direct rebuke keeps the source’s scolding tone.
“Continued in the same low whisper” preserves the delivery without redundant phrasing.
SOL drops the extent in “all the way south of the Yangtze.”
“Let out a faint exclamation” captures the young official’s soft exclamation.
“Wield considerable influence” naturally conveys the family’s regional sway.
“Barely twenty” narrows the age more than the source’s approximate age of twenty.
“Done your homework” is an idiomatic way to say he investigated.
The capital’s established rendering and capitalization are preserved.
The young official’s gaze remains directed at the person behind both men.
“Turned to follow” keeps the slow turn and avoids an unnecessary body-part detail.
The line keeps the narrator’s observation that the words sounded like a scream.
The Son of Heaven title and the Emperor’s descent from Heaven remain clear in natural phrasing.
“Likely to do just that” clarifies the link to the thought of killing them without changing it.
“Flap” better matches the source’s fluttering sound than “Flick,” which suggests a snapping motion.
Naming the man whose voice cuts off makes the source’s action clear without changing it.
SOL drops the source’s description of the Emperor as an absolute ruler.
The ellipsis preserves the stunned pause in natural English punctuation.
The ellipsis preserves the stunned pause in natural English punctuation.
“Trembling” keeps the image of the air quivering.
“Piercing me from head to toe” naturally conveys gazes penetrating his whole body.
The lowly seat, far end of the hall, and distance from the throne all remain.
Italics correctly mark the narrator’s direct thought while preserving the profanity.
“Everyone had staked their lives” preserves the gamble’s stakes without implying only two sides.
The reordered sentence retains the tiger’s-den image and the sense of inevitability.
“Whoosh” better captures the source’s rushing sound than an exhaled “Haaaa.”
“Trembled” preserves the air’s renewed movement.
The emphasis on “trembled” makes the narrator’s correction natural and keeps the meaning.
“Triangular wave” preserves the source’s specific wave image, unlike BASE’s towering wave.
SOL drops the source’s explicit immediacy: the wave hit everyone in an instant.
“Glug” conveys the sound of gulping down the drink.
The revised sentence keeps the action followed by the uproar while improving the flow.
“Had finally hit them” preserves the wave’s impact on people who had doubted its reality.
SOL drops the “high” or heinous-criminal force of 대역 죄인.
“Another fifteen minutes” preserves the additional duration in the source.
SOL drops the explicit method of execution, tearing him apart by quartering.
